Step 4 (what worktrees would NOT fix, read from code, not tested live). .claude/hooks/ledger.mjs resolves its root two ways: `LEDGER_ROOT` env var, else `path.resolve(import.meta.url, '../../..')` - the HOOK FILE'S OWN location. .claude/settings.json wires every hook as `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/ledger.mjs` - for an agent whose cwd is a worktree, CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR is that worktree, so it runs the WORKTREE's own copy of ledger.mjs (git-tracked, checked out same as any file), rooted at the worktree unless LEDGER_ROOT is set. But setting LEDGER_ROOT is not enough by itself: find_task_by_path() walks up from the EDITED FILE's own path, bounded by `dir.startsWith(root + sep)` - an edit inside the worktree never starts with the main tree's path, so the walk-up returns null regardless of LEDGER_ROOT. The auto-log-by-hook path cannot reach the main tree's per-task task.jsonl from a worktree at all; only the agent's own hand-written Write/Edit calls (which new-task already does today, at an ABSOLUTE path per that skill) can reach it - and only if the harness lets an agent write outside its own project root, which is untested here (out of this task's fence: it would need a second real Claude Code session rooted at the worktree, not the plain git command this study used). Skills: .claude/skills/ is also git-tracked, so a worktree minion reads its OWN checked-out copy - stale by however many commits the worktree is behind, same problem as core code. Ports: proven above, just needs a distinct PORT per worktree, nothing structural. Whisper-server and the OS temp scratchpad are outside git entirely - a worktree does nothing for either, they stay one shared instance/directory no matter how many worktrees exist.

decision.about: How a worktree starts from today's real, uncommitted state (1500 porcelain lines: 1377 tracked-modified, 123 untracked)

options.say: The owner commits michael/dev first (even a rough WIP commit)
options.why: fixes it for EVERY future worktree at once and stays fixed until the tree drifts again; free computationally; but it is the owner's action, not the mastermind's or a minion's (never commit is a hard rule) and needs a habit, not a one-time fix

options.say: git diff --binary HEAD > patch.diff + a plain copy of the untracked files, applied fresh into each worktree
options.why: proven today: the TEXT-only diff (2.54 MB) fails to apply - binary files need --binary; the --binary diff (8.6 MB) applied clean (git apply --check, 0 errors) in 0.5s; untracked files (123 files, 48.7 MB) copy with a plain file copy, no git involved. Needs zero rule change and works today, but it is per-worktree overhead (rebuild the patch every time, ~57 MB moved each time) and a snapshot taken mid-edit by another agent could copy in a half-written file

options.say: A standing wip branch the mastermind is allowed to commit to
options.why: most convenient once running (every worktree just branches from wip, no patch-building) but is a rule change to 'never commit' that only the owner can grant, and trades away the safety of the owner being the only one who commits

decision.chose: diff-copy today; commit-first is the fix worth adopting going forward; wip-branch only if the owner wants to revisit the never-commit rule
decision.because: diff-copy is proven, reversible, and needs nobody's permission; commit-first is strictly better once it is a habit, for free; wip-branch is the only one that changes a standing rule, so it waits on the owner

decision.about: How a worktree minion's proven work reaches the live tree

options.say: The mastermind runs `git diff --binary` in the worktree after a boot test/page load/critic passes, then `git apply --binary` in the main tree under one reload hold, then removes the worktree
options.why: the --binary apply was proven clean above; wrapping it in the existing Server/hold.mjs (already built today) gives ONE reload for the whole landed task instead of one per file, which is the owner's reason 1 directly; a conflict (two minions touched the same file) surfaces as `git apply` failing on that one file - loudly, before anything reaches the live tree - which today's single-tree fencing does not do at all: two agents editing one file today just overwrite each other silently, mid-edit, with no detector

decision.because: it reuses a lock that already exists (hold.mjs) and turns a silent collision into a loud, pre-landing one - both directly serve the owner's two stated reasons

decision.about: What the session's reported one-hour prompt-cache TTL changes here
decision.chose: wake the same agent (mastermind, auditor, a landed minion) with SendMessage for any follow-up inside about an hour of its last turn, instead of spawning fresh
decision.because: a landed minion's task notifications here run about 180k-480k tokens; resuming it within the hour serves nearly all of that from the prompt cache (cheap, per this session's own reported TTL) and skips re-reading requirements.md, skills and the touched files cold, which a fresh spawn must do in full at fresh-input price and real wall-clock time. A worktree minion's own long pauses (npm install, a server boot-test, a screenshot loop) also stay warm through the same window instead of risking a cold re-read on the next tool call, which mattered under the old 5-minute default and matters again under this session's 5-minute overage floor. The exact cache-READ price relative to fresh input is UNVERIFIED here - claude --help lists no pricing table and this task did not browse the web to find one, so only the qualitative saving (most of a 180k-480k-token context reused near-free instead of resent) is claimed, not a dollar figure. One separate, locally-verified nuance: claude --help documents --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections, which moves cwd/env/git-status out of the system prompt specifically because they otherwise break cross-session cache reuse - a worktree minion's cwd differs from every other minion's by design, so without that flag each worktree gets its own cache lineage rather than sharing one with its siblings; it does not affect a single agent resuming ITS OWN session, only reuse ACROSS agents.

decision.about: The next step for parallel minions and worktrees

options.say: Keep file fences + today's guards (syntax-guard hook, reload hold, the boot-test in flight) for everything
options.why: zero new moving parts, already working for most edits; but leaves the exact two incidents from today (a shared-module edit, a Server/ edit) with no structural stop - a reload hold is a courtesy each agent must remember, not something that can be forgotten by construction

options.say: Worktrees for Server/ and shared-module edits only - the edits that can take the whole site down - landed by the diff-apply script above; fences stay for everything else
options.why: targets exactly the two incident classes from today with a structural fix (the live tree cannot change until the work is proven and applied under one hold) while leaving the cheap, already-working path alone for ordinary page/module work; costs: the diff-copy overhead per worktree (proven small, ~1s/~57MB today) and the merge script, which is new but small

the cleanest isolation, but pays the diff-copy or commit-first cost on every single task including small ones, and needs the ledger/skills-staleness question (step 4) actually solved, not just reasoned through - premature until commit-first is a habit or the wip-branch rule is granted

decision.because: it is judged directly against the owner's own two reasons: it removes the reload risk (reason 1) exactly where today's two real incidents happened, and it gives collisions a loud pre-landing signal instead of a silent overwrite (reason 2) - without waiting on a rule change or paying worktree overhead for every small edit. Full worktrees-everywhere becomes the better answer once the owner adopts commit-first as a habit (unlocks it for free) or grants a wip-branch rule.

log.msg: Step 2. `git worktree add -b wt-study-experiment ../wt-study HEAD` from the main tree: 2.7s, 6504 files, into C:\Code\lew42\wt-study (a sibling of monorepo, outside the repo). Wrote one dir, `.git/worktrees/wt-study/` (HEAD, index, gitdir, commondir, logs, ORIG_HEAD) - nothing in the main tree's own index touched. `git worktree list` then showed both trees on the same commit 8b4ced8e, the new one on branch wt-study-experiment.

Step 2 continued. Junctioned node_modules in with PowerShell `New-Item -ItemType Junction` (3.7M, instant - cheaper than an install). Booted `PORT=8151 NO_SUPERVISE=1 node server.js` from inside the worktree: listened in under 2s (PID 38236, confirmed by netstat). curl 200 from :8151, and :80 and :8123 answered 200 throughout - the worktree server never touched the ports the owner's site or the mastermind use. Proved real separation, not just a different port: CLAUDE.md differs between the two trees (the main tree's uncommitted edit is invisible in the worktree, which only sees the committed HEAD) - a worktree minion cannot see today's uncommitted work, confirming yesterday's finding still holds. Killed PID 38236 by its own real Windows PID (Stop-Process -Id), confirmed the port cleared (TIME_WAIT only, no LISTENING).

Step 3 (uncommitted-work test, item 2b). Measured the real state: `git status --porcelain` = 1500 lines (1377 tracked-modified, 123 untracked) - matches yesterday's ballpark and confirms michael/dev is still 113 commits ahead of main. `git diff HEAD` (text only) = 2.54 MB, 40956 lines, built in 0.4s. Opened a SECOND short-lived worktree (wt-study-experiment2, same fence - one experiment worktree at a time, both fully removed) with no node_modules junction this time. `git apply --check` on the text-only patch FAILED on every binary file (jpg/png screenshots) - 'cannot apply binary patch ... without full index line'. Rebuilt with `git diff --binary HEAD` (8.6 MB, 0.5s) and `git apply --check` passed clean, 0 errors - so the diff-in approach works but ONLY with --binary, and costs about 8.6 MB / ~1s for today's real diff. Proved the untracked-file half by copying 3 real untracked files (PowerShell Copy-Item, not git) into the second worktree - plain copy, no surprises. Removed the second worktree with --force (git refuses a plain remove once it holds untracked files, which the 3 copies did - expected, forcing your own throwaway worktree is safe) and deleted its branch. Final check: `git worktree list` back to exactly the main tree only, no `.git/worktrees` dir, no wt-study* branch, C:/Code/lew42/ back to just monorepo and scratch_check, node_modules still 68 top-level entries (untouched this round - no junction).

INCIDENT, self-caused, found and fixed within the experiment: removing the junction before `git worktree remove` failed non-interactively (a confirm prompt, no deletion happened - confirmed by the error text). `git worktree remove ../wt-study` then deleted the WHOLE worktree tree recursively and did not treat the node_modules junction as an opaque link - it recursed through it and deleted the MAIN tree's real node_modules contents (confirmed empty by two independent tools, ls and PowerShell Get-ChildItem). Both live servers (:80, :8123) kept answering 200 throughout (already loaded in memory) so there was no visible outage. Fixed at once with `npm install` in the main tree (871ms, 70 packages, restores exactly what package-lock.json already specified - not a new dependency): node_modules back to 3.7M, both servers still 200, package.json/package-lock.json show no diff. This is now the study's strongest concrete finding: a node_modules JUNCTION into a worktree is dangerous on this stack on Windows, because `git worktree remove`'s own cleanup does not special-case NTFS junctions - it walks into them. The safe pattern is a real `npm install` per worktree (871ms here - cheap enough that the junction's speed advantage is not worth this risk), or if a junction is ever used, unlink it with something that respects reparse points (not a recursive delete) and verify with `git worktree list` BEFORE calling `git worktree remove`.

NOTE on the line above: this task never edited .claude/skills/mastermind/SKILL.md - it was only READ (for the addition below). This is the ledger hook's own session-id fallback misattributing a sibling concurrent task's real edit to this task.jsonl, because subagents in one Claude Code session share one session_id and the hook cannot always tell them apart by file path alone. Left alone (out of this task's fence to fix ledger.mjs) - noted here so the record reads honestly. Ironically exactly the kind of shared-tree attribution problem a worktree-per-mastermind would avoid.

ADDITION opened - a 20-minute multi-tier/sub-worktree question from the owner, appended to requirements.md above. Answering from today's own measurements plus reading .claude/skills/mastermind/SKILL.md and .claude/skills/fork-claude-session/SKILL.md - no new experiment on the main tree, no web.

Point 1, FEASIBILITY. Disk: the working tree excluding node_modules and .git is 802 MB (measured, du); .git itself is 217 MB but is SHARED across every worktree of one repo via commondir - it is not duplicated per worktree. So each worktree costs about 802 MB plus a real node_modules install (3.7 MB, proven safe; never junction it - finding above). Nine worktrees: about 7.25 GB total, against 772 GB free on this machine (df) - disk is not a real constraint at nine. Ports: trivial, one private number per worktree, already proven. The diff carry-in (8.6 MB / 0.5s, measured above) is paid once per worktree spun up from the same base state; at nine that is roughly 77 MB and a few seconds total, parallelizable, still trivial. Sub-worktree question (a worktree cut from another worktree's HEAD, plus its uncommitted diff): mechanically YES for the committed part - every worktree of one repo shares the same .git object database and refs, so `git worktree add <path> <branch>` works from anywhere, including pointed at a worktree's OWN branch, once that branch has at least one commit. But the uncommitted part is NOT automatic, for the identical reason proven twice today: a worktree only ever sees committed content. A minion branching its own worktree off a mastermind's worktree needs the same diff-carry-in step again (or the mastermind commits to its own disposable, worktree-only branch first - which is a different, much lower-risk kind of 'commit' than committing on the shared michael/dev, since that branch never touches the main tree except via the diff-apply lander below; still a rule question for the owner, not assumed here).

Point 2, COORDINATION (the pointer design). Smallest version: reuse the EXISTING decision verb (already rendered by the AI board, already used five times in this task) rather than invent a new one - inventing a verb renders as nothing per the new-task skill's own warning. One decision line per claimed target, written by the owning mastermind only, in the MAIN tree's run ledger: id 'own-<target>', options listing each candidate worktree/branch, chose naming which mastermind's worktree owns it right now, status open until landed. Every mastermind reads the whole ledger (cheap - it is what they already read each wake cycle) but writes only ITS OWN lines - append-only means no lock needed, and two masterminds racing to claim the same target just produce two decision lines with the same id at different timestamps, which is itself the visible signal of a collision, exactly like the git apply failure in point 3 of today's original study. The assistant's role stays exactly what today's already-settled verdicts say (owner-dictates/assistant-relays, mastermind-decides-not-asks): it ROUTES (read the ownership lines, send the owner's words to the mastermind that owns that topic by name, via SendMessage), it SUMMARISES (a short status line back to the owner), and it SHOWS (open a comparison page). It must never MERGE (apply any worktree's diff into the main tree itself) or JUDGE between competing versions (pick a winner) - both stay with either the owner directly or a single named lander/mastermind, never the fast lightweight router, because a lesser model deciding between two masterminds' work is exactly the left-hand/right-hand failure the owner is worried about, moved one level down instead of solved.

Point 3, COMPARE-AND-PICK. Mechanically cheap given today's proofs: nine worktrees each on their own port (8151-8159, say - trivial, proven), a comparison page that is a wall of either live iframes (one per port) or headless shots at three widths - 400/1920/3440 already matches this repo's own existing screenshot convention (file names like ux-tags-3440.jpg, stability-1920.png seen in today's git status) - plus each version's one-paragraph rationale pulled straight from its mastermind's own decision line. One Approve click keeps a worktree; the rest are removed with the same `git worktree remove` proven safe today (no node_modules junction). Good for: a design question with real taste in it, where seeing actual alternatives side by side has genuine decision value that words alone do not carry - the owner's own example, a dashboard timeline layout, is exactly this shape. Wasteful for: a bug fix with one right answer - nine independent agents converging on the same correct fix multiplies cost by roughly nine for zero extra decision value, since there is nothing meaningfully different to pick between and the comparison step itself (building the wall, shooting nine screenshots, reading nine near-identical diffs) is pure overhead on top of that.

Point 4, COST, in multiples of 'one Sonnet minion task' (the owner's stated range today: 160k-770k tokens per minion; no dollar figure used, per the brief). Today's actual pattern (Scenario A): 1 Fable mastermind + about 7 Sonnet minions, reportedly hitting the weekly line today (reported by the coordinator; this task independently saw weekly_all climb from 29% to 40% over the day in usage.jsonl, consistent with a busy day but not a precise re-verification of that specific claim) - roughly 7 minion-units plus the Fable mastermind's own orchestration turns, whose exact size is UNVERIFIED here (it reads broad status each cycle but does not build; call it roughly 1 unit as a rough order-of-magnitude placeholder, not a measured figure) - about 8 units total for the day's real output across MANY different targets. Scenario B, one Sonnet assistant + 2 Opus masterminds: the assistant is explicitly designed to keep its own context tiny (its own skill's words) - call it under 0.2 units; 2 masterminds each running the mastermind skill's own stated practical ceiling of about 3-6 minions - at the low end, 2 x (1 orchestration-unit + 3.5 minion-units) is about 9 units, roughly the same raw spend as today's Scenario A but split across only 2 independent targets instead of ~7, and each Opus unit likely costs more per token than a Sonnet unit (Opus is the more capable, pricier tier) - the exact multiplier is UNVERIFIED locally, no pricing table found in claude --help or installed docs. Scenario C, nine Opus masterminds on ONE target (the owner's literal sub-worktree ask): 9 x (1 orchestration-unit + roughly 2 minion-units for a single competing version, fewer than a full campaign since each mastermind is building only one version) is about 27 units, plus the compare-and-pick overhead itself (nine sets of screenshots, a comparison page, reading nine rationales) adds a few more - call it 28-30 units, for ONE target, of which 8 of the 9 produced versions are thrown away. That is roughly 3-4x today's entire day of real output (Scenario A, ~8 units across many targets), spent on a single design question, all at the pricier Opus tier.

decision.about: Whether to run multi-tier compare-and-pick with nine masterminds on one target, now

options.say: Nine Opus masterminds on one target today, worktree-isolated, compare and pick

options.say: Keep today's shape: one Fable mastermind, minions dispatched one at a time, no worktrees, no compare-and-pick
options.why: already working, cheapest, but never actually tests whether compare-and-pick is worth its cost on a real taste question, and does nothing for the left-hand/right-hand worry the owner raised

decision.because: it is the smallest version of the owner's own idea that still produces a real, comparable answer - not nine, not zero - and every open question in points 1 and 2 (does the ledger actually prevent a collision, does foregrounding minions actually keep a sub-mastermind unstuck) gets answered by running it once at N=3 before anyone commits real Opus spend to N=9

log.msg: Point 1 continued, what breaks at nine (read from .claude/skills/mastermind/SKILL.md, not tested live). Two concrete, already-documented harness facts: (a) a nested agent's completion notifies the MAIN session, never its parent - the skill states this exactly and names two Fable sub-masterminds that hit it on 2026-08-21, parked forever awaiting harvest, because they ran their own minions in the background instead of the foreground. At nine masterminds each spawning minions, EVERY one of them must run its own minions in the foreground (run_in_background:false) to receive its own completions directly - any sub-mastermind that backgrounds a minion effectively loses it to the main session and stalls. (b) Sessions message each other by name - SendMessage takes an agent's id or name as its 'to' field (confirmed from this session's own Agent tool description) - this is what makes the ledger's ownership lines useful: a coordinator can look up 'who owns this target' and SendMessage that name directly rather than re-deriving context. (c) The 1-hour cache is per SESSION, not shared across sibling masterminds - nine masterminds are nine separate cache lineages (each pays its own first-turn fresh-context cost, then gets cheap resumes within its own hour), not one shared discount; cost scales close to linearly with mastermind count, not sub-linearly. Also worth naming plainly: the mastermind skill's own line states '~3-6 agents at once is the practical ceiling' for concurrent work today - nine SIMULTANEOUS masterminds alone already exceeds that ceiling before counting a single minion underneath any of them, which is the real-world version of 'what breaks at nine': not git, not disk, but how many independently-running things a human or a lesser-model router can actually track and unstick when one gets parked.

assign.outcome:
**Plain `git worktree add` works, live-tested — and the same test caught a real, self-inflicted mistake and fixed it before it reached anyone.** A private worktree served from its own port while the owner's :80 and the mastermind's :8123 stayed up the whole time; `git diff --binary` applies clean into a fresh worktree (8.6 MB, 0.5s) where a plain diff fails on binary screenshots; `git worktree list` was left exactly as found.

- [Worktree study](/framework/ai/2026-09-19/worktree-study/) — one screen: six findings, a measurements table, five full decision lines (with alternatives) in this task's log.
- **The mistake:** junctioning `node_modules` into the worktree, then removing the worktree, recursed through the junction and emptied the MAIN tree's real `node_modules`. Caught at once, fixed with `npm install` (871ms) before either live server needed it. Going forward: a real install per worktree, never a junction, on Windows.
- **Recommendation:** worktrees for `Server/` and shared-module edits only — today's two actual incident classes — landed by a small diff-apply script under the existing reload hold; everything else keeps today's file fences, which already work.
- **Left open, the owner's call:** commit `michael/dev` regularly to unlock worktrees for every minion for free, or grant a standing branch the mastermind may commit to (a rule change). The exact prompt-cache-read price is unverified locally — no pricing table in `claude --help`; only the qualitative saving (most of a 180k-480k-token context reused near-free on resume) is claimed.

assign.outcome:
**Addition landed: nine masterminds on one target is feasible but oversized — start with three.** Disk, ports and the diff carry-in are all trivial at nine (about 7.25 GB total, proven-safe mechanics from today's experiment). What actually breaks first is coordination: the harness notifies a nested agent's completion to the MAIN session, never its parent, so every sub-mastermind must run its own minions in the foreground or it stalls forever — and nine masterminds alone already exceeds the mastermind skill's own stated practical ceiling of about three to six agents at once.

- The smallest coordination fix reuses what already exists: one `decision` line per claimed target in the main tree's ledger, written only by its owning mastermind; the assistant routes and shows, never merges a diff or judges between versions.
- Cost, in multiples of one Sonnet minion task: today's real pattern is about 8 units across many targets; nine Opus masterminds on ONE target is about 28-30 units, with 8 of 9 built versions thrown away.
- **Recommendation:** not nine — the assistant (already built) plus ONE mastermind running compare-and-pick of THREE worktree versions on the next real design question (the V3 timeline is a candidate), then measure.
- Left open: a headless check found this task's own page (and an untouched sibling page, on both servers) currently renders an empty body because of an unrelated, live breakage in the shared devbar Ask/Dictate loader (three 404s) — not caused by this task; the page's module itself was confirmed sound directly (parses, serves the right content). Likely to clear once that other in-flight edit lands.
